region.name: Engineering Hiring & Compensation
region.summary: Covers engineering talent strategy including job descriptions, candidate evaluations and offers, compensation bands and above-band approvals, referral bonuses and recruiter sourcing, performance review levels, and related budget and runway planning, alongside a stray round-up multiplier experiment result.

brief.text:
This region covers post-Series B engineering hiring and the compensation machinery around it. The offer stage is the main bottleneck: Priya N.'s September 2026 hiring review (data Jun 1 to Sep 30) found application volume roughly 3x May levels, but the offer-accept rate sits at about 55%, and several past declines were comp-related. The canonical successful offer is Sarah Kim (Senior Backend Engineer, 8 years backend experience). Her loop produced 3 strong hires and 1 hire, with one system-design concern about over-engineering. Her offer of $255k base, top-of-band equity and a $20k signing bonus was approved May 22. She accepted Jun 12 and started Jul 7 in the payments pod under Marcus Bell, and she is seen as a potential senior tech lead for a new infra/platform pod within 18 months. The current open case is Ama, an iOS candidate. The recommendation is an above-band offer of $245k base, top-of-band equity and a $15k signing bonus against a competing $250k offer that expires Oct 14. The rationale flags internal pay-equity risk with existing iOS engineers and timing risk, because board approval of revised bands is not until Oct 21. Whether Aleks Varga can approve the above-band offer now is an open todo. Devon Park is another candidate rated a strong hire, noted for asking about ML feature serving.

On bands and budget, a burn and runway analysis projects burn rising from $540k/mo to about $900k/mo by Q3 2027, with runway staying well above the board's 30-month floor. Citing the 55% accept rate, it proposes raising senior iOS and backend bands at a cost of about $140k/yr. The September exec offsite action items (hiring plan, growth experiment criteria, disclosure copy, card issuing design review, 2027 engineering budget) are all done except a senior iOS comp band benchmark owed by Jordan. A June 2026 hiring watchlist flagged iOS pipeline risk and offer-stage risk. Its actions were hiring a contract recruiter, announcing a referral bonus, and revising the senior iOS JD. The interview loop includes a 60-minute fintech-flavored system design problem shared in advance and a 60-minute technical deep dive that combines light pair programming with conversation. Both are tracked as calibration risks.

The Senior Backend Engineer JD sets the culture pitch. It says the company does not offer flashy perks, title hierarchy or hype, and does offer ownership, founder exposure, mentorship, equity and honest feedback. Candidates apply via the careers page with no cover letter, and internal referrals get priority review. The first formal engineering performance review framework, reviewed with Aleks Varga, was introduced because growth past 20 engineers requires defensible pay decisions. It runs twice a year with no 360s, calibration committees or PIPs. Its levels are E2 (mid-level), E3 (senior) and E4 (staff), with no E1. Typical questions this region answers include what band and offer to extend to a candidate, who approves above-band comp, what the offer-accept rate is and why, the status of specific candidates, the runway impact of band increases, and how engineering levels are defined. A stray, unrelated round-up multiplier experiment result is also filed here.
